issues.legal_issue: A court may refuse relief for a breach of natural justice when admitted or indisputable facts leave only one possible and lawful outcome, making relief futile.
material_facts: The government restored an earlier site allotment without giving notice to the corporation then occupying the site.
That earlier allotment had been made to the corporation as a substitute for another site, following a court order that was later recalled.
After the court recalled that order, the corporation was allowed to retain its original site, while the earlier allottee had no site unless its allotment was restored.
The facts establishing the effect of setting aside the restoration order were admitted or indisputable.
issues.conclusion: Although the restoration order was made without notice, the Court refused to quash it because the admitted and indisputable facts permitted only one outcome and setting it aside would be futile and restore an earlier order made without notice.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 32 and 226, breach of natural justice does not invariably require a court to grant relief. Ridge v. Baldwin and S.L. Kapoor v. Jagmohan recognize the importance of natural justice and that prejudice ordinarily need not be separately proved, but S.L. Kapoor also recognizes that a court need not issue a futile writ where admitted or indisputable facts permit only one conclusion and only one outcome is lawful. Gadde Venkateswara Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh supports refusing discretionary relief where quashing an order would restore an unlawful earlier order; Mohammad Swalleh v. Third Additional District Judge similarly supports not interfering where doing so would restore an illegal order. The Court left the broader correctness of the ‘useless formality’ theory undecided.

rule.if: constitutional_review_of_administrative_order and order_made_without_notice and facts_are_admitted_or_indisputable and only_one_lawful_outcome and setting_aside_would_restore_an_unlawful_order

predicates.constitutional_review_of_administrative_: A party sought constitutional-court review of an administrative order.
predicates.order_made_without_notice: The authority made the challenged order without giving notice to a party affected by it.
predicates.facts_are_admitted_or_indisputable: The facts bearing on the effect of granting relief were admitted or not open to dispute.
predicates.only_one_lawful_outcome: The admitted or indisputable facts permitted only one possible and lawful outcome.
predicates.setting_aside_would_restore_an_unlawful_: Setting aside the challenged order would restore an earlier order that was unlawful or made without notice.

issues.definition: When a party seeks constitutional review of an administrative order made without notice, relief may be denied if the relevant facts are admitted or indisputable, only one lawful outcome is possible, and setting aside the order would restore an unlawful earlier order.

issues.legal_issue: When a court recalls an order that caused a change in an administrative allotment, the consequences of that order must be undone by restoring the prior position.
material_facts: A court order led the government to allot a site to one corporation in place of a site previously allotted to another corporation.
The court later recalled the order that had prompted the substitution.
After the recall, the first corporation was allowed to retain its original site.
The government restored the earlier allotment to the second corporation, but did so without notice to the first corporation.
Setting aside that restoration would leave the second corporation without a site and allow the first corporation to retain both sites.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that restitution was required to restore the status quo ante following recall of its earlier order. It allowed the application seeking restoration of the earlier allotment and dismissed the corporation’s application to quash the restoration order.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that recalling its earlier order required restoration of the prior position and that a party could not retain an advantage obtained as a consequence of an order that had been withdrawn. Articles 32 and 226 confer discretionary powers, and Gadde Venkateswara Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh and Mohammad Swalleh v. Third Additional District Judge support refusing relief where interference would revive an unlawful order. The Court also applied the principle that an entity retaining its original site could not additionally claim a substitute site, while the earlier allottee should not lose its site as a result of the recalled order.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_restitution_after_court: A proceeding seeks to undo consequences that followed from a court order that was later recalled.
predicates.administrative_change_followed_recalled_: An administrative change in an allotment was made as a consequence of the court order that was later recalled.
predicates.original_site_restored_to_substitute_rec: The entity that received a substitute site was allowed to retain its original site after the court order was recalled.
predicates.setting_aside_restoration_would_leave_pr: Setting aside the administrative restoration would leave the prior allottee without a site.

issues.definition: When a proceeding seeks restitution after a court order is recalled, the administrative change followed that order, the substitute recipient has regained its original site, and setting aside restoration would leave the prior allottee without a site, the prior position is restored.
